_about: Content map for the reading-library project (see PROJECT_STATUS.md). One entry per source document in cefr/texts/. Drives conversion to reading/{level}/{slug}.html + assets/audio/reading/{level}/{slug}.mp3. Authored from a full read of all 98 extracted source documents, not from filenames. NOTE on source_files: it records where a text came FROM, so the paths stay even where the file is gone. Two things removed files legitimately: the per-text PDFs were retired in Milestone 2 when print/save-as-PDF replaced them (decision D-7's exception), and the DELETE entries were removed outright on the audit's verdict. Neither is a broken link to chase; check_site_integrity.py is what guards the live site.

_fields.words: word count of the .docx-extracted source (docx preferred over pdf per instruction)
_fields.genre: reading | dialogue | drill | discussion | reference — drills/discussions are not reading texts, so audio is n/a
_fields.level: recommended CEFR level after audit (the source library was flat/unlevelled)
_fields.action: KEEP | EDIT | MERGE | SPLIT | RECLASSIFY | CONVERT | REPLACE | DELETE
_fields.status: NOT STARTED | AUDITING | EDITED | CONVERTED | IMPLEMENTED | REVIEWED | COMPLETE

texts.reason: Present perfect applied where it is wrong: 'I've known there are some exciting purchases', 'The salesperson has told me...'. Rewrite the tense scheme. — DONE: Tense scheme fixed. The source narrated a finished day of shopping entirely in the present perfect ('I've come across a laptop', 'The salesperson has told me'), which is ungrammatical for completed events at a known time; it is now past simple narration. The say/speak/talk/tell contrast is kept and tested, including talk AT versus talk TO.

texts.reason: The drill half of the say/speak/talk/tell set; attach to the merged reading. — DONE: Converted into two new exercise blocks on the existing say-speak-talk-tell-02 page rather than a page of its own: a correction block and a past-simple/present-perfect choice block. Two pages already teach these four verbs, so a third would have been duplication.

Strong long-form workplace mystery (2407w) — too long for one page and one audio file. Split into chapters, per requirement 8's guidance against huge audio files. — DONE: VERDICT CHANGED. The audit said split into chapters because of the audio length; the user asked for it kept as one story, so it is one page. The length problem is handled by editing instead — the source's 2,407 words are cut to 1,362 by pruning the similes ('like a lion in a cage', 'a digital tsunami', 'a scowl that could curdle milk'), which brings the recording to 8:25 and 2.9 MB. The source's own glossary of idioms and IT terms becomes the vocabulary, filtered by the no-cognate rule.

New slug is ASCII and hyphen-only, which the source filename's literal '+' was not (P-3).

texts.reason: Charming short story with English names already. Edited: the letter-spacing artifacts from the source layout are gone, the American pinching custom is now explained up front instead of assumed, 'St. Patty’s' is corrected to 'St. Paddy’s', and the original multiple-choice distractors ('an underpaid teacher', 'her single mother', 'she ate dubious medicinal plants') are replaced with real ones — they were snarky rather than pedagogically useful.

texts.reason: Several unrelated short articles ('Robot Birds' and others) in one file; split so each gets its own page, questions and audio. — DONE: split into four pages, each with its own questions and audio — b1/robot-birds, b1/hachiko, b2/intelligence-pills and b2/john-snow. The source's Right / Wrong / Doesn't say format is kept, because the third option teaches something true-false cannot: telling what a text states from what a reader assumes. Each article was fact-checked and updated where it had drifted — Snow's outbreak was 1854 not 1855 and the Board of Health rejected his finding; Hachiko was fed and housed by others, and the present statue is a 1948 replacement; the Liverpool robops and the 'intelligence pills' predictions were both de-dated.

Multiple fables in one file. Split per fable; keep the literary register but gloss the archaic phrasing. — DONE: split into three themed pages rather than seven — what-we-tell-ourselves (fox, dog), what-groups-are-for (sons, travelers, mice) and slow-and-steady (grasshopper, tortoise). VERDICT NOTE: the audit said split per fable, but a fable is a 200-word form and a page holding one is too thin to carry a reading, audio and exercises; grouping by theme also lets the closing paragraphs argue across the fables, which is where the real B2 work is. Archaic phrasing glossed as vocabulary rather than modernised away. Seven Doré, Crane, Bewick and Winter illustrations carried over from the .docx; the eighth was a Warner Bros. cartoon still and was left out on copyright grounds.

texts.reason: Strong functional dialogues, but eight unrelated scenarios in one worksheet (airline booking, reconfirming, passport control, booking a hotel room, checking out, ordering dinner, buying clothes, asking for a photo) with every student line left blank. Split into three coherent pages and given model answers so the dialogues can actually be read and narrated. Americanized throughout per requirement 16: euros to dollars, 24-hour times to 12-hour ('16:45' to '4:45 p.m.'), 'the trout is off' to 'we're out of the trout', 'colours' to 'colors', traveller's cheques to a card; the inconsistent 'Northwind Airways'/'Northwind Airlines' is unified, and the source's acute accents used as apostrophes ('There´s') are fixed.

texts.reason: Both 'Court Trials' files cover famous US cases; merge into one curated reading and even out the register ('some crazy courthouse cases'). — DONE: Merged with trials-mayors into one curated reading. Register evened out ('some crazy courthouse cases' is gone) and the unsubstantiated alternative-suspect theories about the Simpson case are dropped. Two factual additions the sources lacked: the Scopes conviction was overturned in 1926 on a technicality, and the criminal/civil split in Simpson turns on the standard of proof.

texts.reason: Same title and theme as trials, focused on mayoral corruption cases. — DONE: Merged into reading/c1/trials.html as the Kilpatrick case. The source's internal inconsistency (indicted on 24 counts, then 'guilty on 24 of the 30') is resolved.

Good there is/there are practice, but the source crams nine separate grammar points (there is/are, can/could/may, some/any/no, much/many/few/little, present simple, will, present continuous, past simple, question forms) into one narrative, and it breaks down: 'Do you visit the mountains a lot?' is answered 'No, I don't visit the coast often', which is a non-sequitur, and 'I'm reading a map upstairs later' is not English. Rewritten around the one dominant point (there is/are plus quantifiers) and re-set as a Charlotte-to-Asheville bus trip with English names; the other grammar points already have their own lessons under levels/.
texts.card_desc: There is / there are and quantifiers, on a long bus ride into the mountains.
